specStatements.text: Electromagnetic waves are transverse waves that transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber.
Electromagnetic waves form a continuous spectrum and all types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.

The waves that form the electromagnetic spectrum are grouped in terms of their wavelength and their frequency. Going from long to short wavelength (or from low to high frequency) the groups are: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
Our eyes only detect visible light and so detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves.
Students should be able to give examples that illustrate the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves.

concepts.definition: A transverse wave that transfers energy from the source of the wave to an absorber. Electromagnetic waves can travel through a vacuum, so they do not need a substance to travel through.
A wave in which the oscillations are perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transfer. All electromagnetic waves are transverse; sound waves, by contrast, are longitudinal.

The object or device that emits the electromagnetic wave and from which the energy is transferred away. Examples include the Sun, a lamp filament, a radio transmitter, the magnetron in a microwave oven and an X-ray tube.

The object that takes in the electromagnetic wave and receives the energy it carries. Examples include skin warmed by the Sun, water in food in a microwave oven, a solar cell, a receiving aerial and the retina of an eye.

Electromagnetic waves carry energy away from a source and deliver it to an absorber; no matter travels from the source to the absorber. Evidence of the transfer is a change in the absorber, such as a rise in temperature, a current in an aerial or a chemical change in the skin.

The electromagnetic spectrum runs without gaps from the longest wavelengths to the shortest. The seven named groups are convenient labels for regions of one unbroken spectrum, not seven separate kinds of wave, and the boundaries between them are not sharp.
A space containing no matter. Electromagnetic waves travel through a vacuum, which is why light, infrared and ultraviolet from the Sun reach the Earth across empty space.

All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air. Radio waves, visible light and gamma rays from the same event therefore arrive at the same time; the groups differ in wavelength and frequency, not in speed.

The distance from a point on one wave to the equivalent point on the next wave. Wavelength is one of the two properties used to group the electromagnetic spectrum; radio waves have the longest wavelengths and gamma rays the shortest.

The number of waves passing a point each second. Frequency is the other property used to group the spectrum. Across the spectrum, going from long to short wavelength is the same as going from low to high frequency.
Going from long to short wavelength (or from low to high frequency) the groups are: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light (red to violet), ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

The group of the electromagnetic spectrum that lies between infrared and ultraviolet. Within visible light, going from long to short wavelength runs from red to violet, so red has the longest wavelength of the visible colours and violet the shortest.

concepts.term: Limited detection range of the eye
concepts.definition: Our eyes only detect visible light, so they detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves. Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays all reach us unseen and need instruments, not eyes, to detect them.
The waves that form the electromagnetic spectrum are grouped in terms of their wavelength and their frequency — not in terms of their speed, their amplitude or how they are made.

misconceptions.question: Can electromagnetic waves travel through empty space?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. They travel through a vacuum (space) as well as through air.
misconceptions.misconception: Waves need something to travel through, so light must need air — there must be some very thin air out in space carrying it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sound, water waves and waves on a rope are met first, and every one of them needs a substance. The rule 'a wave needs a medium' is over-generalised to light.
misconceptions.correction: Electromagnetic waves are the exception: they travel through a vacuum. Sunlight, infrared and ultraviolet cross millions of kilometres of empty space to reach the Earth, which they could not do if a substance were needed.

misconceptions.question: Do gamma rays travel faster than radio waves through a vacuum?
misconceptions.correct: No. All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma rays have a much higher frequency and are far more dangerous, so they must be travelling much faster than radio waves.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students link 'high frequency' and 'high energy' with 'fast', because in everyday language something high-frequency sounds rapid, and because dangerous things are imagined as fast-moving.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is the same for every group in a vacuum or air. What changes across the spectrum is wavelength and frequency. A radio wave and a gamma ray leaving a distant star together arrive at the Earth together.

misconceptions.question: Are there gaps between the groups of the electromagnetic spectrum?
misconceptions.correct: No. The spectrum is continuous, so the groups run into one another with no gaps.
misconceptions.misconception: There are seven separate types of electromagnetic wave, with nothing in between them — a bit like seven different substances.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook diagrams draw the spectrum as seven coloured boxes with hard lines between them, which looks like seven separate things rather than one unbroken range.
misconceptions.correction: The spectrum is continuous. The seven names label regions of a single unbroken range of wavelengths, and the boundaries are not sharp — waves exist at every wavelength in between.

misconceptions.question: If one wave has a longer wavelength than another, how do their frequencies compare?
misconceptions.correct: The longer wavelength wave has the lower frequency.
misconceptions.misconception: A longer wavelength means a bigger wave, so it must have a higher frequency as well.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Longer' and 'higher' both feel like 'more', so students expect the two quantities to increase together instead of running in opposite directions.
misconceptions.correction: The specification orders the spectrum from long to short wavelength, which is the same order as low to high frequency. Radio waves have the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency; gamma rays have the shortest wavelength and the highest frequency.

misconceptions.question: How much of the electromagnetic spectrum can our eyes detect?
misconceptions.correct: Only visible light — a limited range of electromagnetic waves.
misconceptions.misconception: We can see most of the spectrum, because we can see light and we can also feel and sense the other waves around us.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Diagrams often draw visible light as a wide band across the middle of the spectrum, and 'sensing' warmth or sunburn gets muddled with 'seeing'.
misconceptions.correction: Our eyes only detect visible light and so detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves. Everything else — radio, microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays — is invisible to us and needs a detector.

misconceptions.question: What is infrared radiation?
misconceptions.correct: It is a group of the electromagnetic spectrum — a transverse wave that transfers energy from a source to an absorber.
misconceptions.misconception: Infrared is the hot air coming off something hot; it is heat itself rather than a wave.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Infrared is met through the warmth felt near a fire or a heater, where hot air really is rising as well, so the wave and the moving hot air get merged into one idea.
misconceptions.correction: Infrared is an electromagnetic wave and needs no air at all. Infrared from the Sun crosses a vacuum to reach us, and a person standing to one side of a fire, not above it, still feels the energy arriving.

misconceptions.question: Are electromagnetic waves transverse or longitudinal?
misconceptions.correct: Transverse — the oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer.
misconceptions.misconception: Light and radio waves are longitudinal like sound, because they spread out from a source in the same way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sound is usually the first wave studied in depth, and both sound and light travel outwards from a source, so the type of oscillation is assumed to be the same.
misconceptions.correction: Sound is longitudinal, but every electromagnetic wave is transverse: the oscillation is at right angles to the direction in which the energy is transferred, not along it.

misconceptions.question: Do radio waves transfer energy?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Like every electromagnetic wave they transfer energy from a source to an absorber.
misconceptions.misconception: Radio waves only carry information, such as music or a phone signal — they do not carry energy the way infrared or gamma rays do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Radio waves produce no sensation at all, so there is nothing to feel, and the everyday word for what they do is 'carry a signal' rather than 'transfer energy'.
misconceptions.correction: A receiving aerial absorbs radio waves and an alternating current appears in it. That current is evidence that energy has been transferred from the transmitter to the aerial.

misconceptions.question: Which comes last in the spectrum, X-rays or gamma rays?
misconceptions.correct: Gamma rays — the order ends ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays.
misconceptions.misconception: Gamma rays come before X-rays, because gamma is the one you meet first when learning about radioactivity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In radioactivity the emissions are ordered alpha, beta, gamma, so gamma is remembered as a familiar early item, and the alphabet puts X near the end of the list.
misconceptions.correction: Learn the specification order as one list: radio, microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. Gamma rays sit at the short wavelength, high frequency end.

misconceptions.question: Where does ultraviolet sit in the electromagnetic spectrum?
misconceptions.correct: Between visible light and X-rays, at a shorter wavelength than visible light.
misconceptions.misconception: Ultraviolet is between infrared and visible light, because infrared and ultraviolet are the two invisible ones either side of the middle.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Infrared and ultraviolet are often taught together as 'the invisible ones near light', and their positions are then swapped or merged.
misconceptions.correction: The order is infrared, then visible light, then ultraviolet. The prefixes help: infra means below the red end and ultra means beyond the violet end, so ultraviolet lies past violet, not before red.

misconceptions.question: Which visible colour has the longest wavelength, red or violet?
misconceptions.correct: Red has the longest wavelength; violet has the shortest.
misconceptions.misconception: Violet must have the longer wavelength, because it looks like the deeper, stronger colour.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Colour is judged by how it looks rather than by its place in the spectrum, and the specification's own phrase 'red to violet' is read without noticing that it runs long to short.
misconceptions.correction: The specification lists visible light as 'red to violet' inside a run from long to short wavelength. Red therefore has the longest wavelength and the lowest frequency of the visible colours, and violet the shortest and highest.

misconceptions.question: Can our eyes detect infrared?
misconceptions.correct: No. Our eyes only detect visible light.
misconceptions.misconception: We must be able to detect infrared with our eyes, because we can tell when something hot is nearby.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Warmth from a fire is felt at the same time as its glow is seen, so detecting infrared with the skin gets confused with seeing it.
misconceptions.correction: The skin senses the warming caused by absorbed infrared; the eye does not detect infrared at all. The glow of a fire that we do see is visible light. That is why an infrared remote control beam is invisible.

misconceptions.question: Do electromagnetic waves travel faster in air than in a vacuum?
misconceptions.correct: No. They travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.
misconceptions.misconception: Air helps to carry the wave along, so waves must go faster in air than in empty space.
misconceptions.whyItArises: For sound, a medium is essential, so air is thought of as the thing that carries a wave rather than as something a wave passes through.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states that all types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air. Air is not needed and does not speed the wave up.

misconceptions.question: Does anything travel from the source to the absorber?
misconceptions.correct: Energy is transferred from the source to the absorber; matter is not.
misconceptions.misconception: Tiny particles must move from the source to the absorber, otherwise nothing would arrive.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday transfers involve something physically arriving — post, water, hot air — so students expect a wave to deliver a substance too.
misconceptions.correction: Electromagnetic waves transfer energy, not matter. The evidence that something arrived is the change in the absorber, such as its temperature rising or a current appearing in it.

misconceptions.question: What does it mean to say the electromagnetic spectrum is continuous?
misconceptions.correct: There are no gaps in it — waves exist at every wavelength across the whole range.
misconceptions.misconception: It means the waves are given out continuously, without stopping.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Continuous' in everyday use describes something going on in time, so it is read as a statement about emission rather than about the range of wavelengths.
misconceptions.correction: Here 'continuous' describes the range of wavelengths and frequencies, not the timing. The spectrum runs unbroken from the longest wavelengths to the shortest, whether or not any source is switched on.

misconceptions.question: In which direction is energy transferred by an electromagnetic wave?
misconceptions.correct: From the source of the waves to an absorber.
misconceptions.misconception: The absorber pulls the energy in, so it is the absorber that acts on the source.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Phrases such as 'the plant takes in sunlight' or 'the aerial picks up the signal' put the absorber in the active role, hiding the direction of the transfer.
misconceptions.correction: The wave is emitted by the source and carries energy away from it; the absorber receives that energy. Naming the source and the absorber separately for each example fixes the direction.

mcqs.stem: Which phrase best describes all electromagnetic waves?

options.text: Longitudinal waves that transfer energy to an absorber
options.rationale: A student who has studied sound first assumes every wave that spreads out from a source oscillates along the direction of travel.

options.text: Transverse waves that transfer energy to an absorber
options.rationale: The specification defines electromagnetic waves as transverse waves that transfer energy from the source of the waves to an absorber.

options.text: Transverse waves that transfer matter to any absorber
options.rationale: Picked by a student who thinks something physical must arrive at the absorber for a transfer to have happened.

options.text: Longitudinal waves that transfer matter to an absorber
options.rationale: Combines both errors: the sound-wave model of oscillation and the idea that particles travel from source to absorber.

mcqs.stem: A radio transmitter sends radio waves to the aerial of a car radio. Which statement describes the energy transfer?

options.text: Energy is transferred from the aerial to the transmitter.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks of the aerial as actively 'picking up' the signal and so reverses the direction.

options.text: No energy is transferred, only information is carried.
options.rationale: Radio waves produce no sensation, so students treat them as signal carriers rather than energy carriers.

options.text: Energy is transferred from the transmitter to the aerial.
options.rationale: The transmitter is the source and the aerial is the absorber, so energy travels from transmitter to aerial.

options.text: Energy is carried by particles that leave the aerial.
options.rationale: Picked by a student who believes a transfer requires matter to travel, and who also reverses the direction.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the speed of electromagnetic waves is correct?

options.text: Gamma rays travel faster than radio waves in a vacuum.
options.rationale: Students link high frequency and high danger with high speed, so gamma rays are assumed to be the fastest.

options.text: All types travel at the same velocity through a vacuum.
options.rationale: The specification states that all types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through a vacuum (space) or air.

options.text: Radio waves travel faster than gamma rays in a vacuum.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who reasons that a longer wavelength covers more distance per wave, so the wave must move faster.

options.text: No type of electromagnetic wave can travel in a vacuum.
options.rationale: The rule 'a wave needs a medium', learned from sound, is over-generalised to electromagnetic waves.

mcqs.stem: Ultraviolet and infrared leave the Sun at the same moment and travel through space to the Earth. Which statement is correct?

options.text: They arrive together because both travel at the same speed.
options.rationale: All types of electromagnetic wave travel at the same velocity through space, so equal distances take equal times.

options.text: Ultraviolet arrives first because its frequency is higher.
options.rationale: Higher frequency is wrongly read as faster travel, so the ultraviolet is expected to win the race.

options.text: Infrared arrives first because its wavelength is longer.
options.rationale: A student who muddles wavelength with speed reasons that longer waves must move ahead more quickly.

options.text: Neither arrives, because space has no air to carry them.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who believes every wave needs a substance to travel through.

mcqs.stem: The electromagnetic spectrum is described as continuous. What does this tell you?

options.text: There are exactly seven separate wave types, with gaps.
options.rationale: Diagrams drawn as seven boxes with hard borders suggest seven distinct kinds of wave separated by gaps.

options.text: The waves are all given out continuously and never stop.
options.rationale: 'Continuous' is read as a statement about time rather than about the range of wavelengths.

options.text: There are no gaps between the groups of waves in it.
options.rationale: A continuous spectrum runs unbroken from the longest wavelengths to the shortest; the seven names label regions of one range.

options.text: Every source gives out all seven groups at the same time.
options.rationale: An over-reading of 'continuous' as meaning the whole spectrum is always present from any source.

mcqs.stem: Which list of groups is in order from longest wavelength to shortest wavelength?

options.text: microwave, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet
options.rationale: This is the specification's own order for these four groups, running from long to short wavelength.

options.text: microwave, infrared, ultraviolet, visible light
options.rationale: Picked by a student who places ultraviolet next to infrared because both are invisible.

options.text: infrared, microwave, visible light, ultraviolet
options.rationale: Infrared and microwave are swapped by a student who assumes microwaves must be small, so they come later.

options.text: ultraviolet, visible light, infrared, microwave
options.rationale: The whole list is reversed by a student who thinks the long wavelength end is the high frequency end.

mcqs.stem: A group of the electromagnetic spectrum has a lower frequency than infrared. Which group could it be?

options.text: ultraviolet
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who places ultraviolet just below infrared because both are invisible neighbours of light.

options.text: microwaves
options.rationale: Microwaves lie before infrared in the low to high frequency order, so their frequency is lower.

options.text: X-rays
options.rationale: Picked by a student who reads the spectrum backwards and treats the short wavelength end as the low frequency end.

options.text: gamma rays
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who remembers gamma from radioactivity as an early item and so places it low in the spectrum.

mcqs.stem: Compared with visible light, radio waves have:

options.text: a longer wavelength and a higher frequency
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who expects wavelength and frequency to increase together because both sound like 'more'.

options.text: a shorter wavelength and a lower frequency
options.rationale: Correct on frequency but wrong on wavelength, from a student who thinks radio waves must be tiny to fit in a radio.

options.text: a shorter wavelength and a higher frequency
options.rationale: Picked by a student who has the order of the spectrum reversed and places radio near the gamma ray end.

options.text: a longer wavelength and a lower frequency
options.rationale: Radio waves sit at the long wavelength end of the spectrum, which is also the low frequency end.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the colours of visible light is correct?

options.text: Violet light has a longer wavelength than red light.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who judges wavelength from how deep or strong the colour looks.

options.text: Red light has a higher frequency than violet light.
options.rationale: A student who knows red has the longer wavelength but expects frequency to rise with wavelength picks this.

options.text: Red light has a longer wavelength than violet light.
options.rationale: The specification lists visible light as red to violet within a run from long to short wavelength, so red is the longest.

options.text: Every visible colour has exactly the same wavelength.
options.rationale: Picked by a student who over-applies 'all electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed' to wavelength as well.

mcqs.stem: Which part of the electromagnetic spectrum can the human eye detect?

options.text: Visible light and infrared, which we feel as warmth.
options.rationale: Feeling warmth on the skin is confused with detecting infrared using the eyes.

options.text: Every group in the spectrum, from radio to gamma rays.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks we sense most of the spectrum because it surrounds us all the time.

options.text: Visible light and ultraviolet, which tans the skin.
options.rationale: The visible effect of ultraviolet on skin is mistaken for evidence that the eye detects ultraviolet.

options.text: Visible light only, a limited range of the spectrum.
options.rationale: Our eyes only detect visible light and so detect a limited range of electromagnetic waves.

mcqs.stem: A television remote control sends out infrared. Why can you not see the beam?

options.text: The infrared beam is too dim for your eyes to detect.
options.rationale: A student who believes the eye can detect infrared blames brightness rather than the eye's range.

options.text: Your eyes detect only visible light, not infrared.
options.rationale: The eye's detection range is limited to visible light, so infrared passes unseen however strong it is.

options.text: Infrared travels too quickly for your eyes to detect.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks the groups differ in speed and that speed decides what can be seen.

options.text: Infrared carries no energy, so there is nothing to see.
options.rationale: The idea that only some groups transfer energy is used to explain why nothing reaches the eye.

mcqs.stem: Food placed in a microwave oven becomes hotter. Which statement describes what happens?

options.text: Microwaves transfer heated matter into the food.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks a transfer needs some substance to arrive at the absorber.

options.text: The food absorbs hot air produced inside the oven.
options.rationale: Radiation is confused with hot air, the same confusion made about infrared from a fire.

options.text: The food gives out microwaves that warm the oven.
options.rationale: Source and absorber are swapped by a student unsure which object emits the waves.

options.text: Microwaves transfer energy from the oven to the food.
options.rationale: The oven is the source and the food is the absorber; the temperature rise is evidence of the energy transfer.

mcqs.stem: Sunlight falls on a solar cell and the cell produces electricity. In this energy transfer, the absorber is:

options.text: the solar cell, which takes in the light
options.rationale: The absorber is the object that receives the energy carried by the wave, shown here by the current it produces.

options.text: the Sun, which gives out the light
options.rationale: Source and absorber are swapped by a student who labels the more active-sounding object as the absorber.

options.text: the sunlight travelling through space
options.rationale: The wave itself is mistaken for the absorber, because it is the thing that moves.

options.text: the air between the Sun and the cell
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks air must carry the wave and therefore takes in its energy.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about radio waves transferring energy is correct?

options.text: They carry information only, so no energy is transferred.
options.rationale: Radio waves cause no sensation, so students treat them as signals that carry no energy.

options.text: They transfer energy only once they slow down in air.
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who thinks air changes the speed of electromagnetic waves.

options.text: An aerial absorbs them, so energy reaches the aerial.
options.rationale: The alternating current produced in a receiving aerial is the evidence that energy has been transferred to it.

options.text: They transfer energy by pushing air particles along.
options.rationale: The longitudinal, particle-pushing model of sound is applied to radio waves.

mcqs.stem: The waves of the electromagnetic spectrum are grouped in terms of which two properties?

options.text: wavelength and frequency
options.rationale: The specification states that the waves are grouped in terms of their wavelength and their frequency.

options.text: wavelength and velocity
options.rationale: Chosen by a student who believes the groups travel at different speeds, so velocity could separate them.

options.text: amplitude and frequency
options.rationale: Amplitude is a familiar wave property from graph work and is substituted for wavelength.

options.text: velocity and amplitude
options.rationale: Picked by a student who thinks speed varies between groups and between a vacuum and air.

mcqs.stem: A camper holds their hands near a fire and feels them get warmer. Which pair names the source and the absorber correctly?

options.text: source: the camper's hands; absorber: the flames
options.rationale: The direction of transfer is reversed by a student who sees the hands as doing the acting.

options.text: source: the hot air; absorber: the camper's hands
options.rationale: Infrared radiation is confused with the hot air rising from the fire.

options.text: source: the fire; absorber: the surrounding air
options.rationale: A student who thinks air must absorb the wave first before the hands can be warmed picks this.

options.text: source: the fire; absorber: the camper's hands
options.rationale: Infrared is emitted by the fire and taken in by the hands, whose temperature then rises.
